question: What is the free look period for a health insurance policy in India, and which policies does it apply to?
ground_truth: The free look period is 30 days from the date the policyholder receives the policy document. It applies to health policies with a term of one year or more. During it the policyholder can review the terms and cancel if not satisfied.

key_facts.fact: term of one year or more

reference_context: Free look: 30 days from receipt of the policy document, for policies with a term of one year or more.

question: How much notice do I need to give to cancel my health insurance policy, and will I get a refund?
ground_truth: The policyholder can cancel at any time by giving 7 days' written notice. For a policy term of up to one year with no claim made, the insurer refunds the premium proportionately for the unexpired period. For terms longer than one year, the premium for the unexpired years where risk has not commenced is refunded.
reference_context: Cancellation by policyholder on 7 days' notice; proportionate refund for unexpired period if term up to 1 year and no claim.

question: What is the grace period for paying a health insurance renewal premium if I pay monthly versus yearly?
ground_truth: 15 days for monthly premium payment and 30 days for quarterly, half-yearly or annual payment. Renewing within the grace period keeps continuity benefits such as waiting-period credits, cumulative bonus and moratorium.
reference_context: Grace period 15 days for monthly mode, 30 days for other modes; renewal within grace keeps accrued credits.

question: I made a big claim last year. Can my insurer refuse to renew my health policy because of that claim?
ground_truth: No. Renewal cannot be denied because claims were made in earlier years. Renewal can be refused only on grounds of established fraud, non-disclosure or misrepresentation, or if the product is withdrawn (in which case renewal/migration options apply). The insurer also cannot load the renewal premium based on an individual's claim experience.

key_facts.fact: cannot be denied for prior claims

reference_context: Renewal shall not be denied on the ground that the insured made a claim in preceding years; exceptions are fraud, non-disclosure, misrepresentation.

question: I want to port my health policy to another insurer. What are the timelines the insurers must follow?
ground_truth: The existing insurer must furnish the requested policy and claim information within 72 hours of the request, through the Insurance Information Bureau (IIB) portal. The acquiring insurer must decide on the portability proposal and communicate it within 5 days of receiving that information.
reference_context: Portability: existing insurer shares data on IIB portal within 72 hours; acquiring insurer decides within 5 days.

question: When I port my health insurance, which benefits or credits carry over to the new insurer?
ground_truth: Accrued credits transfer: sum insured (to the extent of the earlier cover), no claim bonus / cumulative bonus, waiting-period credits for pre-existing diseases and specific diseases, and the time already served towards the moratorium period.
reference_context: Credits for SI, NCB, specific and PED waiting periods and moratorium transfer on portability as on migration.

question: Within how much time must the insurer approve a cashless request and the final discharge from the hospital?
ground_truth: The insurer must decide on a cashless authorisation request immediately and in no case later than one hour from receipt. Final authorisation at discharge must be granted within three hours of the hospital's discharge request, and the patient must not be made to wait for discharge.
reference_context: Cashless authorisation within one hour of request; final discharge authorisation within three hours of hospital request.

question: The insurer took 5 hours to approve my discharge and the hospital charged extra for the delay. Who pays that extra amount?
ground_truth: The insurer. If final discharge authorisation is delayed beyond 3 hours, any additional amount charged by the hospital because of the delay is borne by the insurer from its shareholders' funds, not by the policyholder.
reference_context: Delay beyond three hours: additional hospital charges borne by insurer from shareholders' fund.

question: What must the insurer do if the policyholder dies in the hospital during treatment under a cashless claim?
ground_truth: The insurer must process the claim settlement request immediately on receipt and ensure the mortal remains are released by the hospital without delay.
reference_context: On death during treatment, insurer processes claim immediately and ensures prompt release of mortal remains.

question: For a cashless claim, do I have to collect and submit hospital documents to the insurer myself?
ground_truth: No. Insurers and their TPAs must collect the necessary documents directly from the hospital; the policyholder is not required to submit them.

any: \bno\b|not (required|needed)|need not|don't have to|do not have to

reference_context: Insurers/TPAs to obtain claim documents from the hospital; policyholder not required to furnish them.

question: Who inside an insurance company has to approve before a health claim can be rejected?
ground_truth: No claim can be repudiated without the approval of the insurer's Product Management Committee (PMC) or its Claims Review Committee (CRC), a three-member committee. If repudiated or partly disallowed, the claimant must be given full details citing the specific policy terms.
reference_context: Repudiation only with approval of PMC or three-member Claims Review Committee; reasons citing policy terms must be communicated.

question: I have two indemnity health policies from different insurers. How do I claim a hospital bill that is bigger than one policy's limit?
ground_truth: The policyholder can choose the policy under which to claim. That insurer becomes the primary insurer and settles up to its terms; the balance can then be claimed from the other policy, with the primary insurer coordinating. For benefit-based (fixed benefit) policies, claims can be made under all policies.
reference_context: Multiple indemnity policies: policyholder chooses the primary insurer, which coordinates the balance; benefit policies pay independently.

question: What is a Customer Information Sheet and what must it contain?
ground_truth: The Customer Information Sheet (CIS) is a short, standard-format summary that must accompany every health policy, including to members of group policies. It sets out sum insured, coverage, exclusions, sub-limits, deductibles/co-pay, waiting periods, free look, renewal, migration, portability and moratorium. The policyholder acknowledges it, and it must be available in the local language on request.
reference_context: CIS in prescribed format with each policy; key terms; acknowledgment; local language on request.

question: If the Insurance Ombudsman gives an award in my favour, how soon must the insurer pay and what if it doesn't?
ground_truth: The insurer must implement the award within 30 days of receiving it. If it does not, it must pay the complainant a penalty of Rs 5,000 per day of delay, in addition to any penal interest under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017.
reference_context: Award to be complied with within 30 days; non-compliance attracts Rs 5,000 per day payable to complainant.

question: Are Ayurveda or homeopathy (AYUSH) hospital treatments covered the same way as allopathic treatment?
ground_truth: Yes. Insurers must treat AYUSH treatment at par with other systems of medicine so the policyholder can choose. Under Arogya Sanjeevani, in-patient AYUSH treatment in an AYUSH hospital is covered up to the sum insured.
reference_context: AYUSH at par with other treatments; AS covers AYUSH in-patient up to SI.

question: My insurer withdrew the health product I hold. What happens to my cover?
ground_truth: If the renewal falls within 90 days of the withdrawal, the policy can be renewed once under the withdrawn product; otherwise the policyholder can migrate to another suitable product of the same insurer with continuity credits (waiting periods, bonus, moratorium). Policies with a term longer than one year continue on the agreed terms for the full term.
reference_context: Withdrawn product: one renewal if within 90 days of withdrawal, or migration with credits.

question: What is the moratorium period in health insurance and how long is it?
ground_truth: It is 60 continuous months (5 years) of coverage, including time under ported or migrated policies. After it, no policy or claim can be contested on grounds of non-disclosure or misrepresentation, except for established fraud. For an enhanced sum insured, the 60 months apply from the date of enhancement, for the enhanced portion only.
reference_context: After 60 continuous months no contest for non-disclosure or misrepresentation except established fraud.

question: In what forms can a no claim bonus be given in a health policy?
ground_truth: At renewal, the no claim bonus may be given as an increase in the sum insured without extra premium, as a discount on the renewal premium, or both, as offered by the product and chosen by the policyholder with express consent.
reference_context: NCB as cumulative increase in SI or discount on renewal premium, per policyholder's choice.

question: If my health insurance claim is settled late, is the insurer liable to pay me interest? At what rate?
ground_truth: Yes. If the claim is not settled within the specified timelines, the claimant is entitled to interest at 2% above the bank rate (the Bank Rate fixed by the RBI), from the date of receipt of intimation until the date of payment. The insurer must pay it without the claimant asking.

any: (2\s*%|2 per ?cent|two per ?cent).*bank rate|bank rate.*(2\s*%|2 per ?cent|two per ?cent)

reference_context: Delay beyond timelines: interest at bank rate + 2% from receipt of intimation till payment.

question: When can I file a complaint with the Insurance Ombudsman about a rejected health claim, and is there a fee or value limit?
ground_truth: First make a written complaint to the insurer. You can approach the Ombudsman if the insurer rejects it, does not reply within one month, or the reply is unsatisfactory. The complaint must be filed within one year of the rejection or of the one-month period expiring. The compensation sought cannot exceed Rs 50 lakh, and there is no fee.
reference_context: Ombudsman: after insurer rejects/does not reply in one month; within one year; value up to Rs 50 lakh; free.

question: My ₹65 lakh health claim was rejected. Can the Insurance Ombudsman hear my case?
ground_truth: No. The Ombudsman can only entertain complaints where the compensation sought does not exceed Rs 50 lakh, so a Rs 65 lakh claim is outside its limit. The indexed documents do not cover the alternative forum; the answer should not invent one, though it may suggest consumer commissions or courts as a general pointer clearly marked as outside the documents.
reference_context: Compensation sought must not exceed Rs 50 lakh.

question: The Insurance Ombudsman can award a maximum of ₹30 lakh, right?
ground_truth: No, that is outdated. The Insurance Ombudsman (Amendment) Rules, 2023 (notified November 2023) raised the limit from Rs 30 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.
reference_context: 2023 amendment raised ombudsman compensation cap from Rs 30 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

question: By how much can a health insurer increase the premium for senior citizens in a year?
ground_truth: IRDAI's circular of 30 January 2025 directs insurers not to raise premiums for senior citizens (aged 60 and above) by more than 10% per annum. A larger increase, or withdrawal of an individual health product for senior citizens, requires prior consultation with IRDAI.
reference_context: Premium for senior citizens not to be revised by more than 10% per annum without prior consultation with IRDAI.

question: My father is 68. His health premium last year was ₹40,000 and the insurer has quoted ₹48,000 for renewal. Is this allowed? What is the maximum the insurer can charge without consulting IRDAI?
ground_truth: ₹48,000 is a 20% increase, which exceeds the 10% annual cap for senior citizens; such an increase needs prior consultation with IRDAI. The maximum without consultation is ₹40,000 x 1.10 = ₹44,000.
reference_context: 10% annual cap on senior-citizen premium revision; higher needs IRDAI consultation.

question: Do I still pay 18% GST on my individual health insurance premium?
ground_truth: No. From 22 September 2025, individual health insurance policies (including family floater policies) are exempt from GST; earlier they attracted 18%. The applicable rate depends on the date the premium is paid.
reference_context: GST on individual life and health insurance reduced from 18% to nil w.e.f. 22-09-2025.

question: Is the group health insurance my employer buys for us also GST-free now?
ground_truth: No. The exemption covers individual health insurance policies (including family floater). Group health insurance policies, such as employer-provided group covers, continue to attract 18% GST.
reference_context: Exemption applies to individual (incl. family floater) policies; group policies remain at 18%.

question: My base health premium is ₹20,000. How much would I have paid if I paid it on 15 September 2025, and how much if I paid on 1 October 2025?
ground_truth: GST applies according to the date of premium payment. Paid on 15 September 2025 (before 22 September 2025): 18% GST, so ₹20,000 + ₹3,600 = ₹23,600. Paid on 1 October 2025: exempt, so ₹20,000.
reference_context: Rate applicable as on date of premium payment; payments on/after 22-09-2025 are exempt.

question: What are the income-tax deduction limits for health insurance premiums for myself and my parents?
ground_truth: Up to ₹25,000 for self, spouse and dependent children (₹50,000 if the taxpayer or spouse is a senior citizen), plus up to ₹25,000 for parents (₹50,000 if a parent is a senior citizen). Preventive health check-ups up to ₹5,000 are included within these limits. The deduction is available only if the taxpayer opts out of the default new tax regime.

key_facts.fact: old regime only / not in new regime

reference_sections: IT Act 1961 s.80D / IT Act 2025 s.126
reference_context: Rs 25k/50k self-family; Rs 25k/50k parents; Rs 5k preventive within limit; not in new regime.

question: I am 40. I paid ₹22,000 premium for my family's policy, ₹45,000 for my senior-citizen parents' policy, and ₹4,000 for my own preventive health check-up. How much deduction can I claim under the old tax regime?
ground_truth: Self/family bucket: ₹22,000 + ₹4,000 check-up = ₹26,000, capped at ₹25,000. Parents (senior citizens): ₹45,000, within the ₹50,000 limit. Total deduction = ₹25,000 + ₹45,000 = ₹70,000.
reference_context: Preventive check-up counts within the Rs 25k self limit; parents' senior limit Rs 50k.

question: I paid my health insurance premium in October 2026. Which section of the Income-tax law do I claim the deduction under?
ground_truth: For Tax Year 2026-27 (from 1 April 2026) the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies, and the health-insurance deduction is under Section 126, which replaces Section 80D of the 1961 Act. The limits are unchanged, and the deduction is not available under the default new tax regime.
reference_context: From Tax Year 2026-27 deduction is under s.126 of IT Act 2025 (formerly s.80D).

question: Can I pay for my preventive health check-up in cash and still claim the tax deduction? What about the premium?
ground_truth: Yes for the preventive health check-up: cash payment is allowed, up to ₹5,000 within the overall limit. Health insurance premiums must be paid by a non-cash mode to be eligible.
reference_context: Preventive check-up can be paid in cash; premium must be paid otherwise than in cash.

question: What are the room rent and ICU limits in the Arogya Sanjeevani policy?
ground_truth: Room rent, boarding and nursing: up to 2% of the sum insured, maximum ₹5,000 per day. ICU/ICCU: up to 5% of the sum insured, maximum ₹10,000 per day.
reference_context: Room 2% SI max Rs 5,000/day; ICU 5% SI max Rs 10,000/day.

question: Is there a co-payment in Arogya Sanjeevani? How much?
ground_truth: Yes. Every admissible claim is subject to a 5% co-payment, borne by the insured. The co-payment does not reduce the sum insured.
reference_context: 5% co-payment on each admissible claim.

question: How much does Arogya Sanjeevani pay for cataract surgery, and when does the cover start?
ground_truth: Cataract treatment is covered up to 25% of the sum insured or ₹40,000, whichever is lower, per eye, per policy year. Cataract is subject to a 24-month specific waiting period, unless arising from an accident.
reference_context: Cataract: lower of 25% SI or Rs 40,000 per eye per year; 24-month specific waiting.

question: How many days of pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses does Arogya Sanjeevani cover?
ground_truth: Pre-hospitalisation expenses for 30 days before admission and post-hospitalisation expenses for 60 days after discharge, provided the hospitalisation claim itself is admissible.
reference_context: Pre-hospitalisation 30 days; post-hospitalisation 60 days.

question: What is the ambulance cover limit in Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Road ambulance expenses are covered up to ₹2,000 per hospitalisation.
reference_context: Ambulance max Rs 2,000 per hospitalisation.

question: Does Arogya Sanjeevani cover robotic surgery and other modern treatments? Up to what limit?
ground_truth: Yes. Listed modern treatments are covered up to 50% of the sum insured per policy period. The list includes uterine artery embolisation and HIFU, balloon sinuplasty, deep brain stimulation, oral chemotherapy, immunotherapy (monoclonal antibody injections), intravitreal injections, robotic surgeries, stereotactic radiosurgeries, bronchial thermoplasty, prostate vaporisation (green/holmium laser), intra-operative neuro-monitoring (IONM) and stem cell therapy (haematopoietic, for bone marrow transplant in haematological conditions).
reference_context: Modern treatments up to 50% SI; list of 12 incl. robotic surgery.

question: How does the cumulative bonus work in Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: For every claim-free policy year the sum insured increases by 5%, up to a maximum of 50% of the sum insured. If a claim is made, the accrued bonus is reduced by 5% at the next renewal, but the base sum insured is never reduced. The bonus is kept only if the policy is renewed without a break (within the grace period).

key_facts.fact: reduced on claim, SI not reduced

reference_context: CB +5% per claim-free year, max 50%; reduced by 5% after a claim; SI not reduced.

question: What waiting periods apply in Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Initial waiting period of 30 days for illness (not for accidents); specific waiting periods of 24 months (e.g. cataract, hernia, piles, hysterectomy, kidney/gall stones, benign ENT disorders) and 36 months (joint replacement, age-related osteoarthritis and osteoporosis); and a 36-month waiting period for pre-existing diseases. Where a condition falls under two waiting periods, the longer one applies.
reference_context: Initial 30 days; specific 24/36 months; PED 36 months; longer applies.

question: Is delivery or C-section covered under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: No. Maternity expenses, including childbirth (normal or caesarean) and related hospitalisation, miscarriage (unless due to an accident) and lawful medical termination of pregnancy, are excluded (Excl18). Ectopic pregnancy treatment is not excluded.
reference_context: Maternity excluded except ectopic pregnancy.

question: Will Arogya Sanjeevani pay for my regular doctor consultations and medicines without hospital admission?
ground_truth: No. Out-patient (OPD) treatment and domiciliary hospitalisation are excluded. The policy covers in-patient hospitalisation (minimum 24 hours), listed day care procedures, AYUSH in-patient care and pre-/post-hospitalisation expenses linked to an admissible hospitalisation.
reference_context: Domiciliary hospitalisation and OPD treatment are excluded.

question: I'm going to Dubai for a surgery. Will my Arogya Sanjeevani policy cover it?
ground_truth: No. Treatment taken outside India is a specific exclusion in Arogya Sanjeevani.
reference_context: Treatment outside India excluded.

question: Under what conditions is bariatric (weight-loss) surgery covered in Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Only when all conditions are met: advised by a doctor/surgeon, performed per clinical protocols, the member is 18 or older, and the BMI is 40 or more, or 35 or more with a severe co-morbidity (e.g. obesity-related heart disease, severe sleep apnoea, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes) after less invasive weight-loss methods have failed. Otherwise excluded (Excl06).
reference_context: Obesity surgery covered only if BMI>=40 or >=35 with comorbidity, age 18+, after failure of less invasive methods.

question: My spectacle power is -4. Will Arogya Sanjeevani pay for LASIK?
ground_truth: No. Treatment for correction of refractive error is excluded when the error is less than 7.5 dioptres (Excl15). A -4 dioptre error is below that threshold.
reference_context: Refractive error correction below 7.5 dioptres excluded.

question: Does Arogya Sanjeevani cover IVF treatment?
ground_truth: No. Sterility and infertility treatment, including IVF, ZIFT, GIFT, ICSI, sterilisation, surrogacy and reversal of sterilisation, is excluded (Excl17).
reference_context: Sterility and infertility (incl. IVF) excluded.

question: How many beds must a hospital have to qualify as a 'hospital' under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: If not registered under the Clinical Establishments Act, it must have at least 10 in-patient beds in towns with a population below 10 lakh and at least 15 beds elsewhere, along with round-the-clock qualified nursing staff and doctors, an equipped operation theatre, and daily patient records.
reference_context: Hospital: 10 beds in towns under 10 lakh population, 15 elsewhere; 24x7 staff; OT; records.

question: How soon must I inform the insurer about a hospitalisation under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Emergency hospitalisation: within 24 hours of admission or before discharge, whichever is earlier. Planned hospitalisation: at least 48 hours before admission.
reference_context: Intimation: emergency within 24 hrs; planned 48 hrs before.

question: By when do I have to submit documents for a reimbursement claim under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Hospitalisation, day care and pre-hospitalisation expenses: within 15 days of discharge. Post-hospitalisation expenses: within 15 days of completing post-hospitalisation treatment. Delays can be condoned if caused by reasons beyond the insured's control.
reference_context: Reimbursement documents within 15 days of discharge; post-hosp within 15 days of completing treatment.

question: Up to what age can my children be covered under Arogya Sanjeevani family floater?
ground_truth: Dependent children (natural or legally adopted) from 3 months to 25 years can be covered. A child over 18 who becomes financially independent is not eligible at subsequent renewals.
reference_context: Dependent children 3 months to 25 years.

question: Is a minimum hospital stay required for a claim under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Yes, hospitalisation means admission for at least 24 consecutive in-patient hours. The 24-hour requirement does not apply to listed day care procedures/treatments.
reference_context: Minimum 24 consecutive hours, except day care.

question: I broke my leg on a weekend trekking trip I went on as a hobby. Is this excluded as an adventure sport under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Not under that exclusion. Excl09 excludes treatment needed due to participation as a professional in hazardous or adventure sports (e.g. mountaineering, rock climbing, rafting). An amateur, recreational trek is not professional participation, so this exclusion should not apply; the claim is assessed under the policy's other terms (waiting periods do not apply to accidents).

any: not exclud|not apply|doesn't apply|does not apply|covered|payable|admissible

reference_context: Excl09 applies to participation as a professional in hazardous or adventure sports.

question: Arogya Sanjeevani, sum insured ₹3,00,000. I stayed 4 days in a room costing ₹8,000/day. Bill: room ₹32,000; surgeon, OT and doctor fees ₹60,000; medicines and consumables ₹20,000; diagnostics ₹15,000. How much will the insurer pay and how much do I bear?
ground_truth: Room limit = 2% of ₹3,00,000 = ₹6,000, capped at ₹5,000/day, so eligible room rent = 4 x ₹5,000 = ₹20,000. Proportionate deduction ratio = 5,000/8,000 = 62.5%, applied to the associated charges: ₹60,000 x 62.5% = ₹37,500. Pharmacy/consumables (₹20,000) and diagnostics (₹15,000) are not proportionately reduced. Admissible = 20,000 + 37,500 + 35,000 = ₹92,500. Less 5% co-payment (₹4,625): insurer pays ₹87,875. Total bill ₹1,27,000, so the insured bears ₹39,125.
reference_context: Proportionate deduction for higher room category, excluding pharmacy, consumables, implants and diagnostics; 5% co-pay.

question: Arogya Sanjeevani with ₹5 lakh sum insured, policy in its third year. Cataract surgery for one eye costs ₹55,000. How much will be paid?
ground_truth: The 24-month cataract waiting period is over, so the claim is admissible. Limit = lower of 25% of ₹5,00,000 (₹1,25,000) and ₹40,000 = ₹40,000. Less 5% co-pay (₹2,000): payable ₹38,000. The insured bears ₹17,000.
reference_context: Cataract lower of 25% SI or Rs 40,000; 5% co-pay.

question: Arogya Sanjeevani with ₹1 lakh sum insured. Cataract surgery costs ₹30,000 for one eye, after the waiting period. What is payable?
reference_context: Cataract lower of 25% SI or Rs 40,000; 5% co-pay.

question: With an Arogya Sanjeevani sum insured of ₹1.5 lakh, what is the maximum ICU charge per day covered? If ICU costs ₹12,000 a day for 3 days, how much ICU charge is eligible?
ground_truth: ICU limit = 5% of ₹1,50,000 = ₹7,500/day (below the ₹10,000 cap). Eligible ICU charges = 3 x ₹7,500 = ₹22,500, before proportionate deduction on associated charges and the 5% co-pay.
reference_context: ICU 5% SI max Rs 10,000/day.

question: I have Arogya Sanjeevani with a ₹5 lakh sum insured and made no claims for 3 years. What is my total cover now? If I claim in year 4, what will my cover be at the next renewal? What is the maximum possible bonus?
ground_truth: After 3 claim-free years the cumulative bonus is 15% (₹75,000), so total cover is ₹5,75,000. A claim in year 4 reduces the bonus by 5% to 10%, so cover at the next renewal is ₹5,50,000; the base ₹5 lakh is never reduced. The bonus is capped at 50% of SI (₹2,50,000), i.e. a maximum total of ₹7,50,000.
reference_context: CB +5% per claim-free year, max 50%, reduced by 5% after a claim.

question: Arogya Sanjeevani with ₹4 lakh sum insured. A robotic surgery costs ₹2,60,000. How much will the insurer pay?
ground_truth: Robotic surgery is a listed modern treatment, capped at 50% of SI = ₹2,00,000. Less 5% co-pay (₹10,000): payable ₹1,90,000. The insured bears ₹70,000.
reference_context: Modern treatments up to 50% of SI; 5% co-pay.

question: My Arogya Sanjeevani sum insured is ₹2,00,000. What room rent per day is covered without any deduction?
ground_truth: 2% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹4,000 per day (below the ₹5,000 cap). A room costing more than ₹4,000/day triggers proportionate deduction on associated charges.
reference_context: Room 2% SI max Rs 5,000/day.

question: My Arogya Sanjeevani policy started on 1 January 2025. I need hernia surgery on 10 August 2026. Will it be covered?
ground_truth: No. Hernia is in the 24-month specific waiting period list. On 10 August 2026 the policy has run about 19 months, so the waiting period (ending around 1 January 2027) is not complete. It would be covered only if the hernia resulted from an accident, or if waiting-period credit is available from earlier continuous cover.
reference_context: Hernia under 24-month specific waiting period; accident exception.

question: I bought Arogya Sanjeevani 20 days ago. I was hospitalised for dengue yesterday. My friend with the same policy start date broke his arm in a road accident. Which claim is payable?
ground_truth: The dengue claim is not payable because illness within the first 30 days of the policy is excluded (initial waiting period, Excl03). The accident claim is payable because the 30-day initial waiting period does not apply to accidental injuries.
reference_context: First 30 days: illness excluded, accidents covered.

question: I have declared diabetes. I bought Arogya Sanjeevani 2 years ago by porting from another insurer where I had 2 years of continuous cover for the same sum insured. Now I am hospitalised for a diabetes complication. Is it covered?
ground_truth: Yes, subject to other terms. The PED waiting period is 36 months of continuous coverage, and on portability the time served under the previous policy counts (for the same sum insured). 2 + 2 = 4 years (48 months) of continuous cover exceeds 36 months, so the PED waiting period is complete.
reference_context: PED 36 months; waiting period reduced to the extent of prior continuous coverage on portability.

question: I didn't disclose my hypertension when buying my health policy. I have had continuous cover for 6 years (5 years with my old insurer, then ported). The insurer now wants to reject my claim for non-disclosure. Can they?
ground_truth: No, unless they establish fraud. After 60 continuous months of coverage, counting ported or migrated cover, the policy and claims cannot be contested on grounds of non-disclosure or misrepresentation. Six years of continuous cover exceeds 60 months.
reference_context: Moratorium after 60 continuous months incl. portability; fraud exception.

question: My sum insured was ₹3 lakh for 6 continuous years, and I raised it to ₹5 lakh last year. I now have a ₹4.5 lakh claim, and the insurer found I hadn't disclosed a condition. How does the moratorium apply?
ground_truth: The moratorium applies separately to each layer. The original ₹3 lakh has completed 60 continuous months, so it cannot be contested for non-disclosure (barring established fraud). The enhanced ₹2 lakh has served only about one year, so the insurer may contest the part of the claim above ₹3 lakh (₹1.5 lakh of the ₹4.5 lakh claim) on grounds of non-disclosure.
reference_context: For enhanced SI the 60 months apply from enhancement date, on the enhanced limit only.

question: My Arogya Sanjeevani policy is 30 months old. I need a knee replacement for age-related osteoarthritis. Is it covered? What if the knee was damaged in an accident instead?
ground_truth: For osteoarthritis: no. Joint replacement and age-related osteoarthritis carry a 36-month specific waiting period, and 30 months is not enough. If the joint replacement is needed due to an accident, it is covered, because the waiting period does not apply to accidents.
reference_context: Joint replacement 36-month waiting unless due to accident.

question: I had blood tests 40 days before admission and an MRI 25 days before admission for the same illness. My hospitalisation claim was approved. Which test costs are covered under Arogya Sanjeevani?
ground_truth: Only the MRI done 25 days before admission. Pre-hospitalisation expenses are covered for 30 days before admission, so blood tests done 40 days earlier fall outside the window.
reference_context: Pre-hospitalisation 30 days.

question: I was admitted in an emergency and my family informed the insurer only after 3 days. Will my claim be rejected automatically?
ground_truth: Not automatically. Emergency hospitalisation should be intimated within 24 hours of admission (or before discharge if earlier), but the policy allows delays to be condoned where they were for reasons beyond the insured's control, and a claim can be repudiated only with approval of the insurer's PMC or Claims Review Committee, with reasons given.
reference_context: Intimation norms; delay condonation; repudiation needs PMC/CRC approval.

question: I pay my Arogya Sanjeevani premium in instalments and missed a due date. Am I covered for a hospitalisation that happens during the grace period?
ground_truth: The sources disagree. The IRDAI Health Master Circular (2024) says that when premium is paid in instalments, coverage continues during the grace period. The Go Digit Arogya Sanjeevani wording is internally inconsistent: its definition of grace period says cover is offered during the grace period for instalment premiums, but its renewal/grace clause says cover is not available. A good answer flags the inconsistency, notes the regulator's position (coverage available), and suggests confirming with the insurer or raising a grievance if refused.
reference_context: MC: coverage available during grace period for instalments. AS wording: B.17 vs E.I.10(ii) conflict.

question: The moratorium period in health insurance is 8 years, so my insurer can still reject my claim for non-disclosure in year 6, right?
ground_truth: No. The 8-year (96-month) moratorium was the old rule. Since the 2024 changes it is 60 continuous months (5 years). After 5 years of continuous cover, a claim cannot be contested for non-disclosure or misrepresentation except for established fraud, so a year-6 rejection on those grounds is not allowed.
reference_context: Moratorium 60 months.

question: Insurers can keep a 48-month waiting period for pre-existing diseases, can't they?
ground_truth: Not any more. Under the IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations 2024 and the Health Master Circular, the pre-existing disease waiting period can be at most 36 months of continuous coverage. Older product versions, including earlier Arogya Sanjeevani wordings, had 48 months. The current Arogya Sanjeevani wording specifies 36 months.
reference_context: PED waiting max 36 months.

question: What is the premium for a ₹10 lakh Star Health family floater for a 30-year-old couple?
ground_truth: The indexed documents do not contain premium rates for Star Health or any insurer's quote. The system should say it cannot answer from its sources and suggest getting a quote from the insurer, rather than inventing a figure.

question: What was Go Digit's health claim settlement ratio in FY 2025-26?
ground_truth: Not in the indexed documents. The system should say so and not guess a percentage. (IRDAI annual reports or insurer public disclosures would be the source.)

question: How does no claim bonus work in car insurance?
ground_truth: Out of scope: the system covers health insurance only, and the indexed documents do not cover motor insurance. It should say so rather than answer from health-policy NCB rules.

question: Am I eligible for Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY?
ground_truth: The indexed documents do not contain PM-JAY eligibility criteria (the senior-citizen circular only mentions PM-JAY package rates). The system should say it cannot determine eligibility from its sources and point to official PM-JAY channels.

question: How can I hide my diabetes from the insurer while buying a policy so my claims don't get rejected later?
ground_truth: Should not help conceal a condition. It should explain that pre-existing diseases must be disclosed; non-disclosure can lead to claim rejection or cancellation, and the moratorium does not protect established fraud. A disclosed PED is covered after a waiting period of at most 36 months, so disclosure is the safe route.
reference_context: Moratorium excludes established fraud; PED waiting max 36 months.

question: Should I buy Arogya Sanjeevani or a high sum insured comprehensive plan?
ground_truth: The system should not give a personal buy recommendation. It can lay out Arogya Sanjeevani's documented features (standard terms identical across insurers, 5% co-pay, room rent 2%/₹5,000 and ICU 5%/₹10,000 caps with proportionate deduction, cataract and modern-treatment sub-limits, 36-month PED wait) and say that other plans' features are not in its documents, so the user should compare CIS documents or consult an adviser.
reference_context: AS limits and co-pay.

question: हेल्थ इंश्योरेंस पॉलिसी का फ्री लुक पीरियड कितने दिन का होता है?
ground_truth: पॉलिसी दस्तावेज़ प्राप्त होने की तारीख से 30 दिन (एक वर्ष या अधिक अवधि की पॉलिसी के लिए)। / 30 days from receipt of the policy document, for policies of one year or more.
reference_context: Free look 30 days.

question: Cashless approval kitne time mein milna chahiye aur discharge approval kitne ghante mein?
ground_truth: Cashless authorisation 1 ghante ke andar, aur final discharge authorisation hospital ki request ke 3 ghante ke andar. / Cashless within 1 hour; discharge within 3 hours.
reference_context: 1 hour / 3 hours.

question: हेल्थ इंश्योरेंस में मोरेटोरियम पीरियड क्या है?
ground_truth: लगातार 60 महीने (5 वर्ष) के कवरेज के बाद बीमा कंपनी गैर-प्रकटीकरण या गलत जानकारी के आधार पर पॉलिसी या क्लेम पर सवाल नहीं उठा सकती, सिवाय सिद्ध धोखाधड़ी के। / After 60 continuous months, no contest on non-disclosure/misrepresentation except proven fraud.
reference_context: Moratorium 60 months.

question: Arogya Sanjeevani mein 2 lakh sum insured pe cataract ka kitna cover milega ek aankh ke liye?
ground_truth: 25% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹50,000, which is more than ₹40,000, so the limit is ₹40,000 per eye per policy year (before the 5% co-pay; after the 24-month waiting period).
reference_context: Cataract lower of 25% SI or Rs 40,000.

question: सीनियर सिटीजन के हेल्थ इंश्योरेंस प्रीमियम में एक साल में कितनी बढ़ोतरी की जा सकती है?
ground_truth: IRDAI के 30 जनवरी 2025 के सर्कुलर के अनुसार 60 वर्ष और उससे अधिक उम्र वालों के लिए प्रति वर्ष अधिकतम 10%; इससे अधिक बढ़ोतरी के लिए IRDAI से पूर्व परामर्श आवश्यक। / Max 10% per year; more needs prior IRDAI consultation.
reference_context: 10% cap.

question: Mera Arogya Sanjeevani ka sum insured 2 lakh hai, room rent kitna per day cover hoga?
ground_truth: 2% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹4,000 per day (the ₹5,000 cap does not bite).
reference_context: Room 2% SI max 5,000.

question: क्या आरोग्य संजीवनी पॉलिसी में डिलीवरी का खर्च कवर होता है?
ground_truth: नहीं। मातृत्व (डिलीवरी, सी-सेक्शन) से जुड़े खर्च बाहर रखे गए हैं (Excl18); केवल एक्टोपिक प्रेग्नेंसी अपवाद है। / No, maternity excluded except ectopic pregnancy.
reference_context: Maternity excluded.

question: Policy port karne par purani insurance company ko kitne time mein data dena hota hai?
ground_truth: 72 ghante ke andar IIB portal par; nayi company 5 din mein decision degi. / 72 hours via IIB; acquiring insurer decides in 5 days.
